claims.claim: English policing developed from mutual-responsibility groupings (tithings, hundreds, shires) with the constable as the earliest identifiable police officer and the shire-reeve as the ancestor of the sheriff; the watch and ward appeared in large towns during the reign of Edward I (1272-1307) and the office of justice of the peace was created in 1326.

By the eighteenth century English constables commonly hired paid substitutes, night watchmen were largely ineffective, and London had nine uncoordinated police offices, each with three paid justices authorized to employ six paid constables, alongside patrols such as the Bow Street Horse and Foot Patrol.

Robert Peel became Home Secretary in 1822 and in 1829 guided through Parliament an Act for improving the police in and near the metropolis, cited as the Metropolitan Police Act 1829, 1829 c. 44 (10 Geo. 4); the resulting force numbered about 1,000 uniformed men under two commissioners with administrative but not judicial authority, accountable to the Home Secretary and through him to Parliament. Statutes of 1839 and 1856 extended the model to counties and required every borough and county to have a force.

The nine principles popularly called the 'Peelian principles' have disputed provenance: the UK Home Office states there is no evidence of any link to Robert Peel, that they were likely devised by the first Commissioners of Police of the Metropolis, Charles Rowan and Richard Mayne, and that they were set out in the General Instructions issued to every new officer from 1829.

American colonists imported constables and sheriffs; Boston had night watchmen by 1636 and New York's were called the Rattlewatch. Philadelphia's 1833 police ordinance was repealed within two years, Boston created a day force in 1838, the New York legislature authorized the first unified day-and-night police in 1844 (organized the following year, and dated 1845 in the standard list), and Boston consolidated its watch with its day police in 1854.

Southern colonial legislatures enacted slave patrol statutes, in South Carolina during the 1740s and in Georgia in 1757, creating patrols with authority to search the dwellings of enslaved people for weapons, punish those found off a plantation without a pass, and enter houses suspected of harbouring or trading with them; Charleston, Savannah and Richmond ran combined foot and mounted patrols, and in Charleston police costs were the largest item in the municipal budget.

Whether slave patrols constitute the origin of American modern-style policing is an interpretive dispute rather than a settled finding: Williams and Murphy present it as a strong argument attributable to Samuel Walker and Philip Reichel, while the conventional account traces municipal departments from the northern watch. Both institutional lines are documented; their relative weight is contested.

Kelling and Moore (NIJ, November 1988) divide American police history into a political era (from the introduction of police into municipalities in the 1840s to the early 1900s), a reform era (taking hold in the 1930s, thriving in the 1950s and 1960s, eroding in the late 1970s), and an emerging community problem-solving era, while cautioning that the boundaries are not clean.

The reform era's defining features included legitimacy grounded in law and professionalism rather than politics, civil service to end patronage hiring, a narrowed crime-control mission, classical/Taylorist organization, August Vollmer's leadership in the 1920s-30s and O.W. Wilson's role as principal administrative architect, preventive patrol by automobile as Wilson's theory, centralized dispatch and 911, and the 1967 President's Commission recasting police as part of a criminal justice system.

Williams and Murphy (NIJ, January 1990) published a critique in the same series calling the Kelling and Moore analysis 'disturbingly incomplete', arguing that it omits slavery, segregation and racism, treats departments as autonomous rather than as barometers of society, and generalizes from the urban Northeast.

The Kansas City Preventive Patrol Experiment ran from 1 October 1972 to 30 September 1973 across 15 South Patrol Division beats matched on crime, calls for service, ethnic composition, median income and transiency, then grouped into five reactive, five control and five proactive beats (the last patrolled at two to three times the usual level); the three conditions showed no significant differences in crime, citizen attitudes, fear of crime, response time, or satisfaction with response time.

The Kansas City report limits its own finding: it states that it did not show visible police presence can have no impact in selected circumstances, warns that the study does not imply fewer officers are needed anywhere, and reports that officers' noncommitted time was 60 percent in the experiment.

Greenwood and Petersilia's RAND study (R-1776-DOJ, 1975) found that traditional approaches to criminal investigation do not significantly affect the rate at which cases are solved, that most cases are solved by routine administrative procedures, that roughly half of investigative effort could be eliminated or shifted without unduly reducing effectiveness, and that apprehension gains are likelier from more alert patrol units and improved citizen cooperation; it proposed restructuring investigation, including a major offenders unit, rather than eliminating it.

Spelman and Brown's 1981 PERF study of more than 4,000 victims and witnesses in four cities concluded that citizen reporting time, not police response time, most affects the possibility of an on-scene arrest, with rapid response improving apprehension mainly where the crime is reported as it occurs.

Scott's 1981 NIJ study coded 26,418 observed citizen calls in departments across Rochester NY, St. Louis MO and Tampa-St. Petersburg FL into 12 categories: requests for information 21 percent, nonviolent crime 17 percent, assistance 12 percent, public nuisances 11 percent, traffic 9 percent, citizen gives information 8 percent, interpersonal conflict 7 percent, suspicious circumstances 5 percent, medical assistance 3 percent, dependent persons 3 percent, violent crime 2 percent, internal operations 2 percent; fewer than 20 percent of calls concerned criminal incidents as citizens described them.

Scott's report explicitly cautions that departments classify the same incident differently, that category assignment moves the percentages, and that the widely repeated figure of about 80 percent of patrol workload being noncriminal carries that same classification ambiguity even though studies converge on it.

Lum, Koper and Wu (Police Quarterly 25(3), 2022) analysed millions of 911 calls for service across nine U.S. agencies and reported that the amount and range of incidents people call police about are voluminous and that most are not obviously transferable to other organisations or government sectors without significant added resources.

BJS's 2022 Police-Public Contact Survey (NCJ 308847, published October 2024) found that 19 percent of U.S. residents age 16 or older, about 49.2 million people, had police contact in the prior 12 months (7.6 percent police-initiated, 11.2 percent resident-initiated, 2.5 percent traffic-accident related); 58 percent of those whose most recent contact was police-initiated were drivers in traffic stops, and 46 percent of resident-initiated contacts were to report a possible crime.

The National Academies' 2018 review sets out four elements of procedural justice drawn from Tyler's work - voice, neutrality, respect and trustworthiness - and concludes that perceptions of procedurally just treatment are strongly associated with judgements of police legitimacy and cooperation but that the research base is insufficient to establish a causal influence on either (Conclusion 6-4).

The same review concludes that the evidence base on whether procedural justice policing affects crime or disorder is very small, supports no conclusion that it does, and is too small to conclude that it does not (Conclusion 4-11); the committee stresses that insufficient evidence is not evidence of absence and notes stronger causal evidence for procedural justice outside policing.

The 1967 President's Commission itself stated that serious crime is only part of the police function and that officers perform a wide range of complex social, behavioural and political tasks, including peacekeeping in disputes ranging from large-scale rioting to conflicts between spouses.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the nine 'Peelian principles' originate with Robert Peel
positions: Popular and much textbook usage attributes the nine principles directly to Peel and to 1829.
The UK Home Office's published note states there is no evidence of any link to Peel and credits the first commissioners, Rowan and Mayne, with instructions issued to officers from 1829.
A strand of scholarship goes further and treats the nine-item list as a later compilation rather than an 1829 document.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the Home Office position as the sourced one, names the popular attribution as unevidenced, and notes without asserting it that scholarship has questioned the list's date of compilation. The substance of the principles is discussed separately from the authorship claim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The relative weight of the northern municipal lineage and the southern slave-patrol lineage in the origins of American policing
positions: The conventional account, summarized by Kelling and Moore, begins with the 'new police' of Boston 1838 and New York 1845 and traces them from the watch.

Williams and Murphy argue that this reflects a northern urban bias, that southern statutory slave patrols predate it by roughly a century, and, attributing the argument to Walker and Reichel, that a strong case exists that the slave patrols were the first American modern-style policing.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both lineages as documented, presents the slave-patrol-as-origin claim explicitly as an interpretive argument with its attribution, declines to extend it to all American policing, and tells the reader that historians differ on the weighting rather than resolving it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Kelling and Moore three-era periodization is an adequate account of police history
positions: Kelling and Moore present it as a useful interpretation and acknowledge that era boundaries are not clean.
Williams and Murphy, in the same NIJ series, call it 'disturbingly incomplete' for omitting slavery, segregation and racism and for treating departments as autonomous strategists.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the periodization because it is the field's shared vocabulary, and immediately teaches the published criticism, directing students to use it as a comparative framework rather than as a national chronology.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strongly to report procedural justice research
positions: Practitioner and reform literature often reports procedural justice as an established route to legitimacy and cooperation.
The 2018 National Academies review found strong associations but insufficient evidence for a causal conclusion in the policing context, and a very small evidence base on crime effects.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the association as strong, the causal question as open in policing specifically, and the committee's own caution that insufficient evidence is not evidence of absence, and it notes the stronger causal evidence for procedural justice outside policing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact share of police workload that is noncriminal
positions: A widely repeated figure holds that about 80 percent of patrol workload is noncriminal.

Scott's own report shows the figure depends heavily on how departments classify incidents, and his measured distribution puts crime-related calls at under 20 percent while noting substantial per-department ranges.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports Scott's measured percentages with their date and study base, states his classification caveat alongside them, and treats the 80 percent figure as a convergent order-of-magnitude finding rather than a constant. Modern corroboration is given from Lum et al. (2022) and BJS (2022) rather than by projecting 1981 figures forward.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted that 'History And Role Of Policing is a foundational concept' with no historical content of any kind; nothing in it was verifiable because it contained no factual claims about policing.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills terms, not policing terms, and were discarded.
The draft's worked example and question bank tested nothing about policing and were replaced entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft; only the topic title survives.
Set the statutory citation for the Metropolitan Police Act 1829 from legislation.gov.uk (1829 c. 44, regnal 10 Geo. 4) rather than relying on secondary phrasing.
Stated the Peelian principles' provenance as the Home Office states it, rather than repeating the standard attribution to Peel.

Reconciled two date conventions for the New York department: the 1967 Commission records an 1844 unification statute, while the standard list Williams and Murphy use dates the department to 1845. Both are given, with the distinction explained.
Framed the slave-patrol origin claim as the interpretive argument Williams and Murphy attribute to Walker and Reichel, not as an established fact, and refused to extend it to all American policing.
Attached the Kansas City report's own limiting statements to its finding, since the finding is routinely overstated.
Attached RAND's own proposed reforms to its finding, since the study is routinely cited as though it recommended abolishing investigation.
Reported procedural justice as an association with an open causal question, per the 2018 National Academies conclusions, rather than as established causal effect.
Avoided citing any percentage from Lum, Koper and Wu (2022) because the full text could not be retrieved; only the publisher-deposited abstract's claims are used.

Omitted the frequently repeated 911 origin details (Haleyville, Alabama, February 1968) because no authoritative source could be retrieved this session; the lesson says only what Kelling and Moore document about 911 adoption and marketing.

Omitted the term 'thief-taker' as an asserted historical fact because no authoritative source for it could be retrieved this session; the pre-1829 patchwork is described using only what the 1967 Commission's history documents (paid constable substitutes, ineffective night watch, magistrates' police offices, Bow Street patrols).
